notes.meaning: These verses name the final group of towns in the lowland hills, including Nezib, Keilah, and Mareshah. Keilah is well known as the town David later saved from Philistine raiders, and Mareshah was the birthplace of the prophet Micah. Naming each town showed that God gave His people real, physical homes to settle.

This passage assigns the Philistine coastal territory to Judah, running from Ekron and Ashdod down to Gaza and the Brook of Egypt. Although God granted this land to Judah, the Israelites did not fully capture or hold it at this time. It reminded the people that they were called to trust God to help them claim all that He had promised.

The list moves up into the central mountains of Judah, which rose several thousand feet high. The towns here include Jattir and Debir, which was also known as Kiriath-sannah. Caleb and Othniel had earlier conquered Debir, proving that steep mountain strongholds could be won through faith.

This list finishes the first cluster of mountain cities, ending with Holon and Giloh. Giloh later became famous as the home of Ahithophel, the wise counselor who betrayed King David. God marked out all these places so every family in the tribe had a known inheritance.

These verses list a second group of nine mountain towns located around Hebron. The most prominent city is Hebron itself, formerly called Kiriath-arba, which Caleb received as his personal inheritance. Hebron later served as the capital where David began his reign as king.

Ten more towns are named on the eastern side of the hills, sloping toward the dry wilderness. Places such as Maon, Carmel, and Ziph later became famous during the years David hid from King Saul. These rugged lands provided shelter for God's chosen king when his life was in danger.

This group names six towns in the high country north of Hebron, including Halhul and the strong fortress town of Beth-zur. These rocky heights formed an important natural defense line for the tribe of Judah. God placed His people in secure hills where they could build peaceful communities.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that ancient Greek copies of the Old Testament include eleven additional towns here, including Bethlehem, which likely dropped out of the Hebrew text through an early copyist's error.

notes.meaning: Only two towns are listed here, located along the northern border of Judah next to Benjamin. The main city, Kiriath-baal, was also called Kiriath-jearim and later housed the sacred ark of the covenant for twenty years. This quiet border town provided a safe resting place for God's holy chest.

Six towns are listed in the barren wilderness of Judea, which sloped downward to the Dead Sea. Even in this harsh desert, places like En-gedi thrived around fresh water springs, and the City of Salt stood in a salt-rich valley. God sustained life and settlements even in dry, desolate surroundings.

The tribe of Judah failed to drive the Jebusites out of the mountain fortress of Jerusalem, leaving both groups living side by side. This failure was not caused by a lack of power from God, but by the people's lack of faith and willingness to finish the work. Leaving this enemy in the land later brought prolonged conflict and spiritual danger to Israel.
